name: Kingdom of Alwa
summary: The southernmost Christian Nubian kingdom, centred on Soba near today’s Khartoum; it lasted almost a thousand years until the Funj and Arab tribes ended it around 1504.

location.value: Central Sudan along the Blue and White Nile and the Gezira plain between them, with its capital at Soba near today’s Khartoum.

terrain.value: Flat Nile floodplains and clay plains (the Gezira), turning to savanna in the south.

climate.value: Hot, with a summer rainy season that is wetter in the south than in Makuria to the north.

resources.value: Grain (sorghum), cattle, horses, and gold and other goods traded from the south.

disasters.value: Droughts and low Nile floods that caused famine.

population.value: Unknown; one medieval writer said Alwa had more land and people than Makuria.

urbanisation.value: Soba was a large town with brick churches and houses; most people lived in villages along the rivers.

migration.value: Arab tribes moved south into Alwa after about 1300, and later Funj people from the south.

economicBase.value: Farming of sorghum, cattle herding and long-distance trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Nile routes north to Makuria and Egypt; routes east to the Red Sea and south to the Ethiopian highlands.

wealth.value: The 10th-century writer Ibn Selim al-Aswani described Alwa as richer than Makuria.

moneyAndTax.value: No coins of its own; trade was by barter and imported goods; the king took tribute in goods.

inequality.value: Rulers and military elites above farmers and herders.

governmentType.value: A Christian monarchy ruling over many regional lords.

keyRulers.value: Few kings are known by name.

succession.value: Within the royal family; as in Makuria, kingship may have passed through the king’s sister’s son.

institutions.value: The royal court, regional governors, and the Church with bishops at Soba.

stability.value: Long stable, but weakened after about 1300 as Arab tribes settled and the kingdom broke into smaller parts.

eliteConflict.value: Little is known; later sources describe rival local lords as the kingdom weakened.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry and archers; horses were important in war.

majorWars.value: Fall to Funj and Arab tribes (about 1504).

territoryChange.value: Shrank after about 1300 as Arab tribes and local lords took over its northern and eastern lands.

alliancesRivals.value: Close ties with Makuria, its Christian neighbour; later threatened by Arab tribes and the Funj.

scienceEducation.value: Church learning in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian.

openness.value: Open to trade with Egypt, the Red Sea and Ethiopia.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on the Nile, camel and donkey caravans, horses.

religion.value: Miaphysite Christianity from about 580, when the missionary Longinus converted the king.

languageWriting.value: Old Nubian (written in an alphabet based on Greek), with Greek and Coptic used in the Church.

artsArchitecture.value: Red-brick churches at Soba, painted pottery and imported glass.

socialStructure.value: King and nobles, clergy, farmers and herders, and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king and to the Christian faith.

dailyLife.value: Most people farmed sorghum or herded cattle and lived in mud houses along the rivers.

neighbours.value: Makuria to the north, Ethiopia to the east, the Beja in the eastern deserts, and peoples to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Nubian Christianity, linked to the Coptic Church of Egypt.

colonisation.value: None; conquered by African and Arab neighbours.

riseSignals.value: Formed after the decline of Meroë; first recorded in the 500s.

peakPeriod.value: The 900s–1100s, when Soba was described as a rich town with many churches.

declineSignals.value: Arab tribes settled from about 1300 and the kingdom split into smaller lordships.

outcome.value: Soba fell to the Abdallab Arabs and the Funj around 1504; the Funj Sultanate of Sennar took its place.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles; population figures are estimates.
